extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims (product, composition, apparatus, process, product-by-process, computer-implemented) for anticipation and obviousness, including inherency, enablement/operability of prior art, and claim construction issues (functional language, printed matter, materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case when claimed and prior art products are structurally or compositionally identical
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claimed and prior art products are identical or substantially identical in structure or composition, or are produced by identical or substantially identical processes, a prima facie case of either anticipation or obviousness has been established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Best, In re Spada: When the PTO shows a sound basis for believing the products are the same, the applicant has the burden to show they are not. The prima facie case can be rebutted by evidence showing the prior art products do not necessarily possess the characteristics of the claimed product. Example cases: Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner (composition within claimed ranges can anticipate even if properties not disclosed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency presumption for claimed properties/functions when structures are substantially identical
rubrics_metrics.description: When the structure recited in the reference is substantially identical to that of the claims, claimed properties or functions are presumed to be inherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior-art structure would necessarily perform the claimed function, inherency can establish anticipation. Applicant must show the prior art would not perform the method or have the property (e.g., in re Schreiber, failure to specify dimensions undermined applicant's declaration). See MPEP § 2113 for product-by-process burden of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims — identical composition implies same properties
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art teaches the identical chemical structure, the properties applicant discloses and/or claims are necessarily present; 'Products of identical chemical composition can not have mutually exclusive properties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Spada: virtual identity of monomers and procedures sufficed for a prima facie case of unpatentability despite claimed differences in tackiness vs hardness. Applicant needs evidence to show different properties despite identical composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter — nonfunctional printed matter does not distinguish products
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the only difference between a prior art product and a claimed product is printed matter that is not functionally related to the product, the printed matter will not distinguish the claimed product from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical question: does any new and unobvious functional relationship exist between the printed matter and the substrate? Cites In re Ngai, In re Gulack. Example: differing instruction content does not avoid anticipation if the instructions are not functionally related.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims — prior art device anticipates if it carries out the process during normal operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under inherency, if a prior art device, in its normal and usual operation, would necessarily perform the method claimed, then the method claimed will be considered anticipated by the prior art device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re King: device disclosed in prior art used in normal operation inherently performs method claims. Applicant must prove the device would not perform the method (e.g., by data comparing results). See In re Best example where cooling step inherently occurred in prior art handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-of-use claims — new uses of old structures can be patentable only in narrow circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of a new use for an old structure based on unknown properties might be patentable as a process of using; however, if the claim is directed to a result or property of the old composition/structure, the claim is anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Hack, In re May, In re Tomlinson: Finding a new property of an old composition (e.g., nonaddictive property) does not necessarily constitute a patentable new use if the references disclosed the composition for related results. Claims reciting new compounds or unexpected properties may be patentable with evidence of unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims — patentability determined by the product, not the recited process
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims are limited by and defined by the process but determination of patentability is based on the product itself; if the product is the same as or obvious from a prior-art product, the claim is unpatentable even if made by a different process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Thorpe, Amgen v. Roche: courts approve use of 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejections for product-by-process claims. In infringement analysis, however, a product-by-process claim is infringed only by a product made by the recited process. Office should consider structure implied by process steps when relevant (In re Garnero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process — burden shifts to applicant to show unobvious difference once prima facie similarity shown
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a product appearing substantially identical is found and a 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejection made, the burden shifts to the applicant to show an unobvious difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Fessmann, In re Marosi, Ex parte Gray: Patent Office bears lesser burden to make prima facie case for product-by-process; applicant must present evidence (comparisons, unexpected properties, purity differences, etc.) to rebut. Office personnel must explain both anticipation and obviousness aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus claims must be structurally distinguishable from the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to an apparatus must be distinguished from the prior art in terms of structure rather than function; apparatus claims cover what a device is, not what it does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Schreiber, Hewlett-Packard v. Bausch & Lomb. Functional recitations alone do not satisfy structural distinctions; examiners should look for structural limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of operating the device does not differentiate an apparatus claim if structural elements are taught by the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A recitation regarding the manner in which a claimed apparatus is intended to be employed does not differentiate the claimed apparatus from a prior-art apparatus if the prior art teaches all the structural limitations of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ex parte Masham: use/intent recitations (e.g., 'for mixing flowing developer material') are immaterial if the structural elements are present in the prior art; amount of submersion or intended use often immaterial to structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: A prior-art device that performs all claimed functions still may not anticipate if there is any structural difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the prior art device performs all the functions recited in the claim, a structural difference can prevent anticipation; means-plus-function limitations are met only by corresponding structures in the specification or equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Ruskin, In re Donaldson, In re Robertson: courts may construe claims to require specific separate elements (e.g., three fastening elements) and find no anticipation if prior art lacks that structure. Consider means-plus-function claim construction rules (see MPEP §§2181–2186).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented functional claim limitations — broad coverage and obviousness considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional claim language not limited to a specific structure covers all devices capable of performing the recited function; the term 'computer' is broad and not limited absent specific definition; broadly claiming automation of a manual function often does not distinguish over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Paulsen, Leapfrog v. Fisher-Price, KSR, Muniauction: a 'computer' can include calculators if specification supports broad interpretation; implementing known functions on a general-purpose computer can be obvious if predictable; adapting existing devices with commonplace electronics or Internet/browser technologies can be obvious. See MPEP §§2143, 2144.04 for obviousness rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material or article worked upon does not limit apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions relating the apparatus to contents thereof during intended operation and inclusion of material or article worked upon by the claimed structure do not, without more, impart patentability to apparatus claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ex parte Thibault, In re Young, In re Casey: the manner a machine is used or the article it forms is not germane to patentability of the machine itself. This line of cases applies to machinery claims, not product or kit claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials manipulated in a process must be considered in process patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The materials on which a process is carried out must be accorded weight in determining the patentability of a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ex parte Leonard: All claim limitations, including materials, must be considered when weighing differences between claimed invention and prior art for obviousness (see MPEP §2143.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel or nonobvious starting material or end product can affect process obviousness — no per se rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A process yielding a novel and nonobvious product may nonetheless be obvious; conversely, a process yielding a well-known product may be nonobvious. Obviousness requires a fact-specific analysis of the claimed subject matter as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Ochiai, In re Brouwer, TorPharm v. Ranbaxy and illustrative cases: treat product limitations as material limitations in process claims; consider all claim limitations; no automatic per se rules — analyze case-by-case (examples given where processes were found obvious or patentable depending on context and presence/absence of novel catalysts or microorganisms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art is presumed operable/enabling when it expressly anticipates or makes obvious all elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference relied on expressly anticipates or makes obvious all elements of the claimed invention, the reference is presumed to be operable; burden on applicant to rebut presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Sasse and MPEP §716.07: examiners may presume operability of prior-art references that teach all claim elements; applicant must provide facts to rebut (e.g., showing inoperability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure standard does not depend on type or nationality of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of disclosure required within a reference to make it an 'enabling disclosure' is the same regardless of whether the prior art is a U.S. patent, foreign patent, printed publication, or other; nationality is not a basis for discrimination under 35 U.S.C. 102/103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Moreton: apply the same enabling/disclosure standard to all prior art types. See MPEP §2122 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy is not required for prior art enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference provides an enabling disclosure and thus anticipates a claimed invention if it describes the claimed invention in sufficient detail to enable one of ordinary skill to carry it out; proof of efficacy is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Impax Labs. v. Aventis Pharm.: enabling disclosure is about ability to make/use without undue experimentation, not proof that the invention works as claimed. See MPEP §2122.

rubrics_metrics.name: A reference is not enabling if prior unsuccessful attempts to make the compound/composition existed before the date of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If attempts to prepare the compound or composition were unsuccessful before the date of invention, evidence of such unsuccessful attempts can show the reference is non-enabling/inoperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Wiggins (unsuccessful attempts weigh against enablement) and contrasts with In re Donohue where mere fact that publication author did not synthesize the compound was insufficient where patents taught synthesis methods. Applicant can overcome a rejection by evidence of inoperability; facts are fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections may be supported by secondary evidence showing reference is operable
rubrics_metrics.description: A 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection can be made even if the primary reference does not itself teach how to practice the invention; secondary evidence (other patents or publications) can be cited to show public possession/enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Donohue and MPEP §2131.01: examiners may combine references or cite secondary references to establish that the primary reference was enabling for the claimed subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inoperative prior art may still be prior art for obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a reference discloses an inoperative device (non-enabling), it may still qualify as prior art for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Beckman Instruments v. LKB Produkter and Symbol Technologies v. Opticon: non-enabling references can be used in obviousness analyses. Examiners should consider the role of such references in 103 rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds and compositions — enabling prior art requires one skilled in the art to be able to make/synthesize
rubrics_metrics.description: For compounds and compositions, an enabling prior art disclosure requires that one of ordinary skill in the art be able to make or synthesize the claimed compound/composition without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section begins the discussion on what constitutes enabling prior art for compounds and compositions (see following MPEP text and cited cases for application). Evidence of methods or corroborating patents/publications may be necessary to show enablement.
